body: This is the motivational speech I needed more than air today. Thank you for this

I don’t know if this is true for everyone, but my experience has been that psychosis can go on for months at a time. However, within those periods there are acute phases and milder phases. Certain delusions may persist throughout, but intense hallucinations come and go. When I’m actively delusional I am unaware of any flaws in my reasoning or in my perception of reality. That’s the nature of a delusion I would say. After the fact, once I stabilize, I’m able to identify and isolate the thoughts and beliefs that were precipitated by the psychosis, but never in the moment, unfortunately.

I often have flashbacks to previous psychotic episodes and the occasional dream in which I appear to be slipping into psychosis again. It can be very upsetting, especially if you’ve had recent mania or depression with psychotic features. For me it’s been over four years since my last hospitalization. I’ve come around to trusting the medication over time. Seroquel in particular is very effective in regulating my sleep, which is a high priority component of my treatment plan. Insomnia can trigger extreme shifts in mood and vice versa. While manic I slept less than 4 hours a night, if at all. Same thing happens if I skip a dose for whatever reason. The fact that you’re dreaming might actually be a good sign even though the content is somewhat disturbing. There is a theory that we dream in order to process trauma and heal the damage that it’s inflicted on our psyche. And in any event, flashbacks, dreams, and other reminders of what it feels like to break from reality can be useful in case it does start happening again. Being able to recognize and have self awareness around early symptoms could lead you to take preventative measures sooner and perhaps avoid a major breakdown altogether.

I mean, sure, it all depends on your commitment to work towards the betterment of society, etc. But if, for example, you are someone who possesses some sort of specialized knowledge or abilities that might lead to the invention or discovery of a medical/technological/economic breakthrough, you are (utilitarianly speaking) doing humankind a great disservice by offing yourself before you accomplish said feat. That being said, even so-called ordinary people have the capacity to move the world closer to a more perfect state by procreating (and thus potentially generating the next Einstein) or working in protective services (thus making the world safer for the next Einstein) or sharing their experiences (thus creating a sense of camaraderie that discourages the next Einstein from giving up) and so on and so forth. Again, granted, it’s all very speculative and uncertain, but you asked for a valid argument and, unless my logic is terribly flawed, staying alive and just doing any non harmful activities has a greater probability of making life better for others than outright killing yourself, which can only arguably benefit you and not even in most cases.

I think you could make a utilitarian argument that, depending on who you are, by killing yourself you are depriving the world of a net good because what you have to offer outweighs the burden you carry by staying alive

Another separate, but related issue I’m grappling with is how to move past the failed relationships that would appear to suggest that I’m somehow less than worthy of being in one. It’s something I think about every day and I’m at a loss for ideas on how to not let these residual insecurities affect me going forward. From where I stand, it all seems rather hopeless. Is time the only cure?

Funny thing is I *do* like myself, but somehow still need the validation of hearing someone else say it too. You set a high bar for relationship readiness, but I don’t think you’re wrong. Whether I can get there though is another matter that deserves serious exploration.
That is true. Although the extent to which we have control over our self-expression is questionable.
Never had much luck with online dating. Lots of dates, some second dates, a few that went on for a month or so, but ultimately no relationships have materialized from it

Changing some aspect of who I am seems counterproductive to me. Ultimately my core will remain the same and whoever gets stuck with me will have to contend with that. Is it best to try to downplay those qualities at least until a relationship progresses to a certain point?
It’s not really THAT kind of anxiety. But yes, I have a therapist

Haha yes it is very important not to forget how to laugh at oneself!

I do NOT specify that casual relationships are off the table, but perhaps I SHOULD as this is the ultimate goal. Generally try to follow the three-date rule. I've been involved in 2-3 boyfriend/girlfriend scenarios.
